title: AI dives into a sea of data, from plankton to pollution

headline: AI Dives Into Sea Of Data
author: Tom Cassauwers

pages.text: Plankton are tiny sea creatures. They are very important for our planet. They help clean the air by taking in carbon dioxide. They are also the start of the food chain for fish. Jean-Olivier Irisson is a scientist who studies them.

He says they are beautiful. Studying plankton is hard work. Scientists look at water samples under microscopes. There are millions of tiny things to count. Doing this by hand takes a very long time. Now, scientists use AI to help them.

AI can look at millions of pictures very fast. It helps scientists identify different organisms quickly. This is a big change for research. It makes the work much easier. Many scientists have this problem. Underwater cameras take many photos of oceans and rivers.

There is too much data for people to check alone. An EU project called iMagine helped solve this. It brought together experts from 11 countries between 2022 and 2025. They created new AI tools to study aquatic data. These tools help us see problems like pollution faster.

evidence: Plankton are not just fascinating to look at.
Researchers collect water samples and examine them under microscopes.
With AI, we can, however, do this very fast.
A1-A2.headline: AI Helps Study Life in the Sea

pages.text: Plankton are essential to marine ecosystems, yet they are often overlooked. Jean-Olivier Irisson, a scientist at Sorbonne Université, highlights their beauty and their critical role in regulating Earth’s climate. By performing half of the world’s photosynthesis, these organisms sustain the entire marine food chain. However, studying these creatures is a painstaking task.

Researchers must manually identify and classify millions of organisms from water samples. Irisson notes that for a single dataset, his team manages 2.2 million images. Manually classifying such a volume is impossible, but AI has transformed this process, allowing for rapid identification and opening new research possibilities. This challenge extends beyond plankton.

Modern underwater cameras and sensors generate vast amounts of data, far exceeding human analytical capacity. To address this, the EU-funded project iMagine brought together experts from 11 European countries between 2022 and 2025. The collaboration aimed to develop AI tools capable of processing large volumes of aquatic data. The project’s impact is significant.

Faster monitoring allows scientists to detect issues like litter accumulation, oil spills, and coral degradation much sooner. By sharing these AI tools and datasets, the project ensures that researchers across Europe can build upon existing knowledge rather than starting from scratch, ultimately supporting broader efforts to restore the health of our oceans and waterways.

evidence: They are fundamental to marine ecosystems, and play a crucial role in regulating Earth’s climate by helping remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
“For a single dataset we have 2.2 million of these images of individual organisms.
Making sense of that flood of information was the goal of iMagine, an EU-funded research collaboration between aquatic scientists and digital experts from 11 European countries.
B1-B2.headline: AI Dives Into Sea Of Data

pages.text: The study of marine plankton, while scientifically vital, presents a formidable logistical challenge. Jean-Olivier Irisson of Sorbonne Université emphasizes that these organisms are not merely aesthetic subjects; they are the bedrock of marine ecosystems and primary drivers of global carbon sequestration. Despite their importance, the methodology for monitoring them has historically been labor-intensive, requiring researchers to manually classify millions of specimens captured in water samples.

The advent of artificial intelligence has fundamentally altered this landscape. Irisson reports that his team’s processing of 2.2 million images, once a multi-year endeavor, is now achievable in a fraction of the time. This technological shift is critical, as modern environmental monitoring—utilizing underwater cameras and sensors—produces data streams that are far too voluminous for manual interpretation.

The iMagine project, an EU-funded initiative spanning 2022 to 2025, sought to bridge this gap by fostering collaboration between aquatic scientists and digital experts from 11 European countries. The project’s objective was to develop robust AI tools capable of analyzing large-scale aquatic data. This innovation is essential for the timely detection of environmental stressors, including plankton decline, litter accumulation, oil spills, and coral degradation.

By democratizing access to these AI models and training datasets, iMagine has enabled a broader scientific community to leverage advanced computational resources without the need for redundant development. As Europe moves toward initiatives like the 2030 goal of the EU Mission: Restore our Ocean and Waters, these AI-driven methodologies are becoming indispensable.

They facilitate a more granular understanding of ecosystem shifts and recovery efforts, such as the impact of artificial reefs on biodiversity. Ultimately, the integration of AI into aquatic science is not merely an efficiency upgrade; it is a necessary adaptation to the complexities of modern environmental monitoring, ensuring that policymakers and researchers can respond with greater agility to the evolving state of our oceans and waterways.

evidence: “Half of the photosynthesis in the world is done by plankton,” said Irisson.
That’s impossible to classify manually. With AI, we can, however, do this very fast.
Faster and cheaper monitoring means problems like plankton decline, litter accumulation, oil spills and coral degradation can be picked up and acted on sooner.

title: How AI could replace animal testing
sourceTitle: How AI could replace animal testing
headline: AI Could Replace Animal Testing Methods
author: Anthony King
attribution: This article was originally published in Horizon, the EU Research and Innovation magazine. Original reporting by Anthony King; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: Every year, the EU uses 150 000 animals to test if chemicals are safe. Most of these animals are rats and mice. Many people want to stop this because it is bad for animals. Also, animal tests do not always show how chemicals affect humans.

Researchers are now working on new ways to test chemicals. They want to use AI and human cells instead of animals. This work is part of a big project called ASPIS. It has 60 million euros to find better ways to test safety.

Professor Mathieu Vinken says that only 50 % of animal tests are good for understanding humans. Testing on animals is also very expensive and takes a long time. Scientists say that AI will play a major role in strongly reducing animal testing in the future.

The goal is to keep people safe without hurting animals. Scientists are using new technology to see how chemicals change cells. This helps them understand if a chemical is dangerous. They hope these new methods will replace old tests soon.

evidence: Around 150 000 animals, mostly rats and mice, are used in the EU each year to test the safety of everyday chemicals, but that is starting to change.
The research was carried out as part of ASPIS, the EU’s €60 million research cluster on next-generation chemical safety testing.
AI will play a major role in strongly reducing animal testing in the future.
A1-A2.headline: AI May Reduce Tests on Animals

pages.text: The European Union is moving toward new methods for chemical safety testing, aiming to reduce the 150 000 animals used annually for this purpose. While animal welfare remains a primary concern, researchers also highlight that animal results do not always accurately predict human reactions.

Consequently, the EU has invested 60 million euros into the ASPIS research cluster to develop non-animal alternatives. Professor Mathieu Vinken, who leads the ONTOX initiative within ASPIS, notes that only about 50 % of animal tests are representative of human biology. Furthermore, chronic toxicity testing—which examines the effects of long-term exposure—is both costly and time-consuming.

As Professor John Colbourne explains, the sheer volume of new chemicals entering the market each year makes traditional testing unsustainable, as it can cost up to 15 million euros per substance. To address these challenges, scientists are utilizing AI and organ-on-a-chip technology to interpret how chemicals affect human cells.

These methods aim to identify subtle cellular changes that could lead to long-term health issues like cancer. While completely replacing animal testing is not yet possible, researchers believe that integrating AI and human-relevant data will significantly decrease the reliance on animal models by 2026 and beyond.

evidence: “Maybe 50 % of the animal tests we do are representative for humans,” said Mathieu Vinken, a professor of toxicology at Vrije Universiteit Brussel in Belgium.
“These animal tests are really expensive, especially chronic toxicity tests,” Vinken said, explaining that they can involve hundreds of animals.
“If it takes up to €15 million per substance and three to seven years, and we have thousands of substances to test, then we simply must do something differently,” he said.
B1-B2.headline: AI Could Replace Animal Testing Methods

pages.text: The paradigm of chemical safety assessment in the European Union is undergoing a significant transformation. Historically, approximately 150 000 animals have been utilized annually to verify the safety of consumer chemicals. However, ethical concerns regarding animal welfare, coupled with the scientific limitation that animal models are not always representative of human physiological responses, have catalyzed a shift toward more sophisticated, non-invasive methodologies.

This transition is supported by the ASPIS research cluster, a 60 million euro initiative dedicated to pioneering next-generation safety testing. The economic and temporal burdens of traditional testing are substantial. Chronic toxicity assessments, which evaluate the consequences of long-term, repeated exposure, are particularly resource-intensive. Professor Mathieu Vinken of Vrije Universiteit Brussel emphasizes that these tests can involve hundreds of animals and are often prohibitively expensive.

Professor John Colbourne, who leads the PrecisionTox initiative, notes that the current influx of thousands of new chemicals annually renders traditional, animal-based protocols obsolete. With costs reaching 15 million euros per substance, the necessity for a more efficient, AI-driven framework is clear. Current research, including the ONTOX and RISK-HUNT3R projects, focuses on integrating computational tools with in vitro models, such as organ-on-a-chip technology.

By analyzing how chemicals interfere with conserved biological mechanisms across species, researchers aim to predict long-term toxicity—including potential carcinogenic or reproductive risks—more accurately than traditional rodent models. While total elimination of animal testing remains a future objective, the integration of AI and human-relevant data is already facilitating a substantial reduction in animal usage. This evolution in toxicology seeks to establish a more reliable, ethical, and cost-effective approach to safeguarding both human health and the environment.

evidence: Traditional animal tests can identify immediate toxic effects, but assessing the consequences of long-term exposure is much harder.
Some diseases can develop after years of exposure to chemicals that cause subtle changes in cells, potentially increasing cancer risk or damaging reproductive health.
In the 1940s to 1960s, when animal testing became established, no one anticipated the sheer number of chemicals that would eventually need to be assessed.

title: Building climate resilience into the heart of Europe’s cities
sourceTitle: Building climate resilience into the heart of Europe’s cities
headline: Building Climate Resilience in European Cities
author: Valérie Gillet
attribution: This article was originally published in Horizon, the EU Research and Innovation magazine. Original reporting by Valérie Gillet; SAGA AI-assisted educational adaptation
editorialState: Machine screened and source-attributed; not a guarantee of semantic accuracy

pages.text: Climate change is a big problem for many cities in Europe. Old buildings and roads were not made for today's weather. Now, there is more rain and very hot summers. A survey says that over 80% of cities have climate problems. Dr. Clemente Fuggini is an engineer.

He leads a project called MULTICLIMACT (2023–2027). He works with people from nine countries. They want to help cities stay safe. They do not have one simple answer for everyone. Instead, they make flexible plans for each city. The team has four test sites.

In the Netherlands, they look at flood risks. In Barcelona, they look at heat and rain. They use plants to cool the streets. In Italy, they help fix old buildings after the 2016 earthquakes. They want to make buildings strong but keep their history.

The project helps leaders know where to spend money. They want cities to work well even when there is a disaster. Dr. Fuggini says that resilience is about people and their communities. It is important to be ready for the future.

evidence: Climate change is forcing many European cities to rethink how they are designed and managed.
According to a recent global survey , over 80% of cities report facing significant climate hazards.
The MULTICLIMACT team brings together researchers, engineers and local authorities from nine European countries to assess the range of challenges facing European cities.
A1-A2.headline: European Cities Prepare for Climate Change

pages.text: European cities are currently facing significant pressure as climate change alters weather patterns. Infrastructure designed for past conditions is struggling to cope with heavier rainfall and hotter summers. According to a recent global survey, over 80% of cities report facing significant climate hazards. Dr. Clemente Fuggini, an Italian engineer, is leading the EU-funded MULTICLIMACT (2023–2027) initiative.

The project brings together experts from nine countries to develop flexible methods for urban resilience. Rather than proposing a one-size-fits-all solution, the team creates strategies tailored to local geography and specific risks. The project operates across four pilot sites. In the Netherlands, researchers are using sensors to predict flood risks.

In Barcelona, they are testing nature-based solutions, such as green vegetation and drainage channels, to combat urban heat and flash floods. Meanwhile, in Camerino, Italy, the team is helping to reconstruct historic buildings damaged by the 2016 earthquakes, ensuring they are safer while preserving their cultural identity. The project emphasizes a systemic approach.

Dr. Fuggini notes that resilience relies on an intricate interplay between individuals, communities, institutions and infrastructures. By identifying where limited resources can have the greatest impact, the researchers aim to help cities recover more effectively from disruptions. Ultimately, the goal is to protect not just buildings, but the communities that rely on them.

evidence: Infrastructure built for the weather conditions of the past is increasingly being tested by heavier rainfall, hotter summers and more frequent extreme weather.

Rather than proposing a one-size-fits-all solution, the researchers are developing flexible methods that cities can adapt to their own geography and infrastructure, and to the specific climate risks that they face.
In Camerino, central Italy, the researchers are helping to guide the reconstruction of historic buildings damaged by the 2016 earthquakes.
B1-B2.headline: Building Climate Resilience in European Cities

pages.text: Climate change is compelling European municipalities to fundamentally reassess their urban design and management strategies. Infrastructure, originally engineered for historical meteorological conditions, is increasingly failing under the strain of intensified precipitation, extreme heatwaves, and frequent environmental volatility. Data from a recent global survey indicates that over 80% of cities are currently grappling with significant climate-related hazards. Dr. Clemente Fuggini, an Italian engineer specializing in urban resilience, is coordinating the EU-funded MULTICLIMACT (2023–2027) initiative.

This collaborative effort integrates researchers, engineers, and local authorities from nine European nations to evaluate diverse urban vulnerabilities. Eschewing monolithic solutions, the project develops adaptable frameworks that cities can customize according to their unique geographical and infrastructural constraints. The initiative utilizes four pilot sites to demonstrate practical applications. In the Netherlands, the focus is on predictive modeling for flood mitigation.

Barcelona serves as a case study for urban heat island effects and flash flooding, where the team is implementing nature-based solutions, such as vegetation-based drainage systems, to enhance environmental quality. Concurrently, in Camerino, Italy, the project is guiding the reconstruction of historic structures impacted by the 2016 earthquakes, balancing structural reinforcement with the preservation of cultural heritage. A critical component of this research is the systemic perspective it adopts. Dr. Fuggini asserts that resilience relies on an intricate interplay between individuals, communities, institutions and infrastructures.

By synthesizing data from various urban sectors, the team aims to provide planners with the evidence required to allocate limited resources efficiently. This holistic approach recognizes that urban stability depends on the continuity of essential services during crises. As climate change accelerates, the project seeks to establish a common framework for European cities to enhance their adaptive capacity, ensuring that the focus remains on the long-term resilience of the communities inhabiting these urban environments.

evidence: For Dr Clemente Fuggini, an Italian engineer whose research focuses on the resilience of cities and critical infrastructure, cities and their communities urgently need to work together to face the challenges of a changing climate.
To see how this works in practice, they have set up four pilot sites across Europe, each representing a different climate challenge.
Climate resilience presents a particular challenge for Europe’s historic buildings, where improving safety and energy performance must go hand in hand with preserving centuries of cultural heritage.
